::: {.protected-content}

Spillover describes the diffusion of regime-favored narratives into
public discourse through mechanisms that do not rely on explicit
coordination, direct state control, or coercive amplification. Unlike
traditional propaganda or high-intensity information manipulation
campaigns, spillover mechanisms operate in the background, often
imperceptibly, embedding manipulated or ideologically loaded narratives
into the epistemic routines of everyday media consumption. Their power
lies in subtlety: they exploit systemic vulnerabilities in how
information is sourced, circulated, and socially validated to extend the
reach and legitimacy of regime interests without triggering the
defensive reflexes typically associated with overt state messaging.

Spillover functions through multiple discrete but overlapping
techniques. Each leverages different facets of the modern information
ecosystem—from attribution ambiguity to infrastructural dependency—to
enable authoritarian narratives to appear organic, credible, and widely
shared.

## Discussion

Spillover represents one of the regime's most insidious and structurally
effective tools of narrative diffusion. It avoids overt confrontation,
instead operating through saturation, ambiguity, and integration into
the ambient rhythms of daily communication. By embedding manipulated
content within the routine operations of journalism, social media, and
civic discourse, spillover allows regime-aligned narratives to circulate
widely, appear organic, and resist direct refutation.

Adding noise—the repeated, low-friction recirculation of ideas—adds
atmospheric density, creating the illusion of consensus through sheer
presence. Together, these mechanisms dissolve the distinction between
independent thought and managed perception, subtly reshaping the
informational environment while remaining difficult to trace.

:::
